content: After discharge, the child should be weighed weekly to monitor progress. If the child fails to gain weight over a two-week period, loses weight between measurements, develops a loss of appetite, or shows signs of oedema, they should be referred back to the hospital for further evaluation. Following discharge from nutritional treatment, periodic monitoring is essential to prevent relapse. A mortality audit should be maintained, including a register of admissions, discharges, and deaths. This register should document details such as the child’s weight, age, sex, date of admission, date of discharge, or date and time of death. To identify modifiable factors that could improve care, it is important to analyze whether most deaths occurred within 24 hours (potentially due to untreated or delayed treatment of hypoglycemia, hypothermia, septicemia, severe anemia, incorrect rehydration fluids, or overuse of IV fluids) or within 72 hours (possibly due to excessive feeding volumes during refeeding or incorrect formula). It is also necessary to check whether potassium and antibiotics were administered appropriately. At night, consider hypothermia due to insufficient covering or lack of night feeds. When transitioning to F-100 or RUTF, assess whether the transition from starter to catch-up feeds was too rapid. During rehabilitation, weight gain should be standardized and measured accurately on the hospital ward. Scales should be calibrated daily, and children should be weighed in the morning after removing clothing (while avoiding hypothermia). Weight gain is categorized as poor (<5 g/kg/day), moderate (5–10 g/kg/day), or good (>10 g/kg/day). If weight gain is less than 5 g/kg/day, determine whether this is a widespread issue among all treated children (indicating a need for a major review of case management) or specific to individual cases (requiring reassessment as if they were new admissions). If weight gain is poor, evaluate feeding adequacy. Ensure that night feeds are provided and that target energy and protein intakes are met. Accurately record the amount of food offered versus what was left uneaten. Recalculate feeding quantities as the child gains weight. Assess whether the child is vomiting or ruminating. Review feeding techniques to ensure frequent feeds in unlimited amounts. Evaluate the quality of care provided by staff, ensuring they are motivated, gentle, loving, and patient. Check all aspects of feed preparation, including scales, ingredient measurements, mixing, taste, hygienic storage, and adequate stirring to prevent separation. Ensure complementary foods are energy-dense enough and that multivitamin composition and shelf life are adequate. Verify the preparation and administration of mineral mixes. If complementary foods are provided, confirm that they include an electrolyte/mineral solution. If feeding is adequate and there is no malabsorption, suspect a hidden infection if there is a recurrence of oedema, hypoglycemia, or hypothermia. Commonly overlooked infections include urinary tract infections, otitis media, tuberculosis, and giardiasis. In such cases, re-examine the child carefully, repeat urine microscopy for white blood cells, examine stool samples, and, if possible, perform a chest X-ray. Consider treatment even in the absence of a confirmatory diagnosis. Children with HIV/AIDS can recover from malnutrition, but recovery may take longer, and treatment failures are more common. Initial nutritional treatment for severe acute malnutrition in children with HIV/AIDS should follow the same protocol as for HIV-negative children. For other HIV-related conditions, refer to specific guidelines. Children with HIV may require special attention, including love and care, to address behaviors such as self-stimulation through regurgitation or attention-seeking. Encourage mothers to spend time playing with their children to foster emotional well-being. Management of specific conditions in HIV-infected children is generally similar to that in other children. However, infections in HIV-positive children may be more frequent, severe, and recurrent, and some may be caused by unusual pathogens. Many HIV-positive children die from common childhood illnesses, which can often be prevented through early diagnosis, proper management, routine vaccinations, and improved nutrition. These children are at higher risk for staphylococcal and pneumococcal infections and tuberculosis. Early identification, immediate treatment with antiretroviral therapy (ART), and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis are critical for saving lives. All infants and children should have their HIV status determined at their first contact with the healthcare system, ideally at birth or as soon as possible thereafter. Hospitals providing maternal, neonatal, and child services should offer HIV testing to mothers and their children. The clinical expression of HIV infection in children is highly variable. Some children show severe HIV-related symptoms within the first year of life, while others remain asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic for years. Perinatally infected children not on ART typically fall into one of three categories: rapid progression (25–30%), with most dying before their first birthday; early symptom development followed by a downhill course, with death by age 3–5 years (50–60%); or long-term survival beyond 8 years (5–25%), often with lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis, stunting, and low weight and height for age. Suspect HIV infection if a child presents with recurrent infections, oral thrush lasting more than 30 days despite treatment, chronic parotitis, generalized lymphadenopathy, unexplained hepatomegaly, persistent or recurrent fever, neurological dysfunction, herpes zoster, or HIV dermatitis. Chronic otitis media, persistent diarrhea, and moderate or severe acute malnutrition are also common in HIV-infected children but can occur in those without HIV. Breastfed infants under 6 months who fail to thrive should raise suspicion for HIV. HIV testing and counseling should be offered to all children attending clinical services in countries with generalized HIV epidemics. If the child’s HIV status is unknown, counsel the family and offer diagnostic testing. HIV testing should be voluntary, with informed consent obtained beforehand. Diagnostic testing in children under 18 months is challenging due to the presence of maternal antibodies. Virological testing is the most reliable method for diagnosing HIV in this age group. Positive virological tests at 4–8 weeks are sufficient to diagnose HIV infection, and ART should be initiated without delay. Negative results in breastfeeding infants should be confirmed 6 weeks after breastfeeding cessation. Clinical staging helps determine the degree of immune system damage and guides treatment planning. Higher clinical stages indicate poorer prognosis, but initiating ART with good adherence significantly improves outcomes.
